summary:
Once found along the tidal rivers and sandy shores of Southeast Asia — from Thailand's southern reaches to the mangrove-edged coasts of Borneo and Sumatra — the Painted Batagur was a creature of quiet, ancient beauty. Its vivid markings made it one of the most striking freshwater turtles in the world.

But human appetite proved relentless. Collected for meat, robbed of its eggs, and displaced by sand mining that stripped away its nesting beaches, this turtle has vanished from most of its former range. Populations have collapsed by at least 80% within just three generations. What remains clings to existence in scattered, fragmented pockets — a species not yet gone, but hovering at the edge of forever.
